## Housekeeping/setup {.smaller}

```{r setup}

# the code below will load the necessary packages for these slides
# packages are normally loaded using library(packageName) after installing them.
# the `pacman` package has a function called `p_load` that checks if a package is 
# installed. If it isn't installed, it will install it, otherwise it will load it.

# this line installs the pacman package, if you need it
if(!require(pacman)){
  install.packages(pacman)
  library(pacman)
}

pacman::p_load(countdown)
pacman::p_load(MASS)
pacman::p_load(tidyverse)
pacman::p_load(datasauRus)
pacman::p_load(ggpubr)
pacman::p_load(wesanderson)
pacman::p_load(patchwork)

# data setup
data(birthwt)

birthwt$smoke = factor(birthwt$smoke, 
                       levels = 0:1, 
                       labels = c("Nonsmoker", "Smoker"))

birthwt$race = factor(x = birthwt$race, 
                      levels = 1:3, 
                      labels = c("White", "Black", "Other"))

birthwt$low = factor(x = birthwt$low, 
                     levels = 0:1, 
                     labels = c("No", "Yes"))

```

## `geom_histogram()` {.smaller}
::: notes
- Default bins = 30
- Note that bins is *not* in `aes()` since it always a fixed number not related to any data
:::

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}
- Continuous variable on the x-axis, divided into equally spaced bins.
- Height of a bar displays the number of observations that fall in each bin.

```{r geom-hist1}
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Histogram of birth weight, roughly bell-shaped and centered around 2800-3300 g, with a tall spike near 2500 g and a few sparse outliers below 1000 g and above 4500 g."

histPlot.bwt = ggplot2::ggplot(birthwt, 
                               aes(x = bwt)
                               ) + 
  ggplot2::geom_histogram()
histPlot.bwt

```
:::

:::{.column width="50%" .fragment}
```{r geom-hist2}
#| code-line-numbers: "3"
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Overlapping histograms of birth weight by race (White, Black, Other, outlined in red, green, blue respectively), all overlaid on the same axis. All three groups show similar bell-shaped distributions centered around 2500-3500 g, with the red (White) outline reaching the highest peak (17) near 2500 g."

ggplot2::ggplot(birthwt, 
                aes(x = bwt, 
                    color = race)) + 
  ggplot2::geom_histogram()

```

```{r geom-hist3}
#| code-line-numbers: "3-4"
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Overlapping semi-transparent histograms of birth weight by race (White, Black, Other), all sharing the same axis, drawn with 100 narrow bins. The finer binning makes each distribution look noisier and more jagged than the 30-bin version, though White (red) still shows a broad peak around 2500-3000 g, with Black and Other (green, blue) more concentrated toward the middle of the range."

ggplot2::ggplot(birthwt, 
                aes(x = bwt, 
                    color = race, fill = race)) + 
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(alpha = 0.7, bins = 100)

```
:::

::::

## `geom_density()` {.smaller}
::: notes
- Additional information on how density estimation occurs in documentation
:::

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}
- Continuous variable on the x-axis.
- Smoothed version of a histogram.

```{r geom-density1}
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Density plot of birth weight, roughly bell-shaped with a peak around 3000-3100 g and a slight shoulder near 2500 g."

densityPlot.bwt = ggplot2::ggplot(birthwt, 
                                  aes(x = bwt)
                                  ) + 
  ggplot2::geom_density()
densityPlot.bwt

```
:::

:::{.column width="50%" .fragment}
```{r geom-density2}
#| code-line-numbers: "3"
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Overlaid density curves of birth weight by race, all sharing the same axis. Black (green) peaks earliest and highest around 2400-3000 g. Other (blue) peaks around 3200 g. White (red) is shifted right with a peak near 3000-3700 g."

ggplot2::ggplot(birthwt, 
                aes(x = bwt, 
                    color = race)) + 
  ggplot2::geom_density()

```

```{r geom-density3}
#| code-line-numbers: "3-4"
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Overlapping filled density curves of birth weight by race, all sharing the same axis. Black (green) peaks earliest and highest around 2400-3000 g. Other (blue) peaks around 3200 g. White (red) is shifted right with a peak near 3000-3700 g."

ggplot2::ggplot(birthwt, 
                aes(x = bwt, 
                    color = race, fill = race)) + 
  ggplot2::geom_density(alpha = 0.6)

```
:::

::::

## `geom_boxplot()` {.smaller}
::: notes
- Thick middle line = median; thinner lines: 25%tile and 75%tile; dashed lines = "whiskers" to +/- 1.5*IQR
- Points beyond 1.5*IQR are given separate dots
- Theme removes ticks and axis text on the right example. Will learn more in the future.
:::

- Continuous variable on the y- or x-axis provides visualization, as well as measures of central tendency and spread.

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r geom_bp1}
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Boxplot of birth weight for all observations. Median around 3000 g, interquartile range roughly 2400-3500 g, whiskers extending from about 1000 g to 5000 g, with one low outlier near 700 g."

ggplot2::ggplot(birthwt, aes(y=bwt)) + 
  ggplot2::geom_boxplot()

```
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r geom_bp2}
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Boxplot of birth weight (bwt) by mother's race (Other, Black, White), with each race shown in a different color and line style, and an outlier point for Other and Black."

ggplot2::ggplot(birthwt, aes(x = bwt, y = race, 
                             color = race, 
                             fill = race, 
                             linetype = race)) + 
  ggplot2::geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.25, 
                        linewidth = 1)

```
:::

::::

## `geom_scatter()` {.smaller}
::: notes
- extensively reviewed in examples
:::

- Two continuous variables (x- and y-axis), continuous or categorical variables for aesthetics.
- Can plot categorical variables on axes but not as informative.

```{r geom-scatter}
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of birth weight vs. mother's pre-pregnancy weight, with point shape indicating race (circle=White, triangle=Black, square=Other) and color shade indicating number of physician visits in the first trimester (ftv, dark=0 to light blue=6). Most points are dark (low ftv), scattered broadly with no clear trend by lwt; a few lighter, high-ftv points appear scattered among the mid-to-high lwt range."

ggplot2::ggplot(birthwt, aes(x = lwt, y = bwt) ) + 
  ggplot2::geom_point(aes(color = ftv, shape = race))

```

## `geom_violin()` {.smaller}
::: notes
- Violin plots look "similar" to boxplots but identify differences in the distributions
:::

- Hybrid between a boxplot and density plot.
  - Displays the distribution and probability density of the data.
  - Mirrored and rotated density plot.
- "Width" of the violin represents frequency of the data points in a given area.
  - Wider sections indicate higher density.

```{r geom-violin}
#| output-location: column
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Violin plot of birth weight by race (White, Black, Other). White shows the widest, most spread-out distribution; Black is narrower and shifted lowest; Other falls in between."

violinPlot.bwt.race = birthwt |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(y = bwt, 
                      x = race, 
                      color = race) 
                  ) + 
  ggplot2::geom_violin(
    aes(fill = race), 
    alpha = 0.4
    )

violinPlot.bwt.race

```

## Layering geoms: Scatterplot example {.smaller}
::: notes
Overlay points and a trend line on the same plot to make the trend clearer against the raw data.
:::

- Geoms can show similar or complementary information about the data 
  - We can combine multiple `geom_*()` functions into a single plot.

```{r layers1}
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of birth weight vs. mother's pre-pregnancy weight, colored by smoking status, with smoothed trend lines and confidence bands overlaid. Raw points are scattered broadly with no clear individual trend, but the smoothed lines show nonsmokers (red) staying slightly above smokers (teal) through most of the range, converging at high weights."

birthwt |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = lwt, 
                      y = bwt) ) + 
  ggplot2::geom_point(aes(color = smoke)) + 
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(aes(color = smoke))

```

## Layering geoms: Order matters

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r layers2}
#| code-line-numbers: "5-7"
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Violin plots for birth weight by race (White, Black, Other), with violins drawn first and boxplots layered on top, so the boxplots are fully visible over the violins."

birthwt |> 
  ggplot(aes(y = bwt, 
             x = race, 
             color = race) ) + 
  geom_violin(aes(fill = race), 
              alpha = 0.4 ) + 
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.2) + 
  theme_classic() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r layers3}
#| code-line-numbers: "5-7"
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Same violin/boxplot pairs by race, but with boxplots drawn first and violins layered on top, so the violin shapes partially cover the boxplot edges."

birthwt |> 
  ggplot(aes(y = bwt, 
             x = race, 
             color = race) ) + 
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.2) + 
  geom_violin(aes(fill = race), 
              alpha = 0.4 ) + 
  theme_classic() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```
:::

::::

## Statistical transformations {.smaller}
::: notes
- geom_boxplot(stat = "boxplot") is the default
:::

Some geoms apply statistical transformations to the supplied data prior to plotting. E.g.,

  - `geom_boxplot` calculates a five-number summary.
  - `geom_bar` counts the number of observations per group.
  - `geom_smooth` fits a regression model and plots its predictions.

Every geom has a default (implicit) stat. Even those that don't perform transformations (`stat = identity`).

. . .

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r transformation1}
#| code-line-numbers: "3"
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Boxplot comparing birth weight by smoking status. Nonsmokers have a higher median (~3100 g) and wider range (1000-5000 g) than smokers, whose median is lower (~2800 g) with one low outlier near 700 g."

birthwt |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(y = bwt, x = smoke)) + 
  ggplot2::geom_boxplot()

```
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r transformation2}
#| code-line-numbers: "3"
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Boxplot comparing birth weight by smoking status. Nonsmokers have a higher median (~3100 g) and wider range (1000-5000 g) than smokers, whose median is lower (~2800 g) with one low outlier near 700 g."

birthwt |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(y = bwt, x = smoke)) + 
  ggplot2::geom_boxplot(stat = "boxplot")

```
:::

::::

## Implicit statistical transformations {.smaller}
::: notes
- Top: count n obs per smoke x race group 
- LHS: geom_bar(stat = count) -> default
- RHS: using precalculated counts w geom_bar(stat = "identity")
- Both plots are the same
:::
- `stat = "count"` is the default for `geom_bar`.

```{r transformation3}
#| output-location: "column"
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Stacked bar chart of counts by smoking status, colored by race (White, Black, Other). Nonsmokers (~115 total) are mostly Other, with smaller White and Black segments. Smokers (~74 total) are mostly White, with smaller Black and Other segments."

birthwt |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = smoke, 
                      fill = race) ) + 
  ggplot2::geom_bar() # default: stat = "count"

```

::::{.columns .fragment}

:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r transformation4}

bw.smoke.race.count = birthwt |> 
  dplyr::group_by(smoke, race) |> 
  dplyr::count()
bw.smoke.race.count

```
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r transformation5}
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Stacked bar chart of counts by smoking status, colored by race (White, Black, Other). Nonsmokers (~115 total) are mostly Other, with smaller White and Black segments. Smokers (~74 total) are mostly White, with smaller Black and Other segments."

bw.smoke.race.count |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = smoke, y = n, 
                      fill = race)) + 
  ggplot2::geom_bar(stat = "identity")

```
:::

::::

## Aesthetics of stat transformations {.smaller}
::: notes
- LHS: color is inherited into both geoms
- RHS: color is only in the point geom so group line plotted
:::


::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r transformation6}
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of birth weight vs. mother's pre-pregnancy weight, colored by smoking status, with separate smoothed trend lines and confidence bands for each group. Nonsmokers (red) trend slightly above smokers (teal) through most of the range, converging at high weights."

birthwt |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = lwt, 
                      y = bwt, 
                      color = smoke) ) + 
  ggplot2::geom_point() + 
  ggplot2::geom_smooth()

```
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r transformation7}
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Same scatterplot and point coloring by smoking status, but with a single smoothed trend line (blue) and confidence band fit to all points combined, ignoring the group distinction — showing an overall rising trend that flattens in the middle range."

birthwt |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = lwt, 
                      y = bwt) ) + 
  ggplot2::geom_point(aes(color = smoke) ) + 
  ggplot2::geom_smooth()

```
:::

## Facets
- Facets generate multiple small plots each showing different subsets of the data.
- Helps compare variables based on a conditioning variable. 
  - E.g., the relationship between age and birthweight *given* smoking status and/or race.
- Conditioning variable must be categorical.
  - Discretize continuous variables.

## Types of facets {.smaller}
There are three types of facets:

- `facet_null()`: generates a single plot (the default). 
- `facet_wrap()`: "wraps" a 1d set of panels into 2d.
- **`facet_grid()`: produces a 2d grid of panels defined by two variables.**
  - One variable for rows and one for columns.

![](figs/01_position-facets.png){fig-alt="Comparison of facet_grid and facet_wrap layouts. Left (facet_grid): a 3×3 grid with columns A, B, C and rows 1, 2, 3, cells labeled by combination (A1, B1, C1, etc.). Right (facet_wrap): the same 3×3 grid with panels simply numbered 1–9 in reading order." height=250 fig-align=center}

We will primary concern ourselves with `facet_grid()` as it can work for one or two faceting variables.

## `facet_grid()` {.smaller}
- Formula syntax: `facet_grid(rowVar~columnVar)`

```{r facet1}
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Grid of scatterplots (birth weight vs. mother's pre-pregnancy weight) faceted by race (White, Black, Other) and smoking status (Nonsmoker, Smoker). Points are scattered broadly in all panels with no clear trend; the White/Nonsmoker panel has the most points, while Black panels have the fewest."

birthwt |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = lwt, y = bwt) ) + 
  ggplot2::geom_point() + 
  ggplot2::facet_grid(smoke~race) # facet: smoke (row) by race (column)

```

## Facets vs. aesthetics {.smaller}
- Compare using only aesthetic combinations (left) to combining facets *with* aesthetics (right).

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r facet2}
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of birth weight vs. mother's pre-pregnancy weight, with point shape indicating race (circle=White, triangle=Black, square=Other) and color indicating smoking status (red=Nonsmoker, teal=Smoker). Points are broadly scattered across all combinations with no clear trend visible by race or smoking status."

birthwt |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = lwt, y = bwt) ) + 
  ggplot2::geom_point(aes(color = smoke, 
                          shape = race))

```
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r facet3}
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Grid of scatterplots (birth weight vs. mother's pre-pregnancy weight) faceted by race (White, Black, Other) and smoking status (Nonsmoker in red, Smoker in teal), with point shape also indicating race. Points are broadly scattered in all panels with no clear trend; White/Nonsmoker has the most points, Black panels have the fewest."

birthwt |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = lwt, y = bwt) ) + 
  ggplot2::geom_point(aes(color = smoke, 
                          shape = race)) + 
  ggplot2::facet_grid(smoke~race)

```
:::

::::

## Facets with fixed layout {.smaller}

```{r facet4}
#| code-line-numbers: "3-4"
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Grid of scatterplots (birth weight vs. mother's pre-pregnancy weight) faceted by race (White, Black, Other) and smoking status (Nonsmoker, Smoker), with faded gray points showing the full dataset in every panel and colored points (red=Nonsmoker, teal=Smoker) highlighting each panel's specific subgroup. Highlighted points are broadly scattered with no clear trend."

birthwt |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = lwt, y = bwt) ) + 
  # plot all points in grey and fix them across facets
  ggplot2::geom_point(color = "grey", alpha = 0.5, layout = "fixed") + 
  # plot all points and color by smoke no fixed layout -> will be faceted
  ggplot2::geom_point(aes(color = smoke, shape = race)) + 
  ggplot2::facet_grid(smoke~race)

```

## Column-only vs. row-only facets {.smaller}
- `. ~ var` column-wise facet.
  - Good for comparison of the y-axis because the vertical scales are aligned.
- `var ~ .` row-wise facet.
  - Good for comparison of the x-axis because the horizontal scales are aligned.

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r facet-columns}
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-align: center

birthwt |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = lwt, y = bwt) ) + 
  ggplot2::geom_point() + 
  ggplot2::facet_grid(.~smoke)

```
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r facet-rows}
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-align: center

birthwt |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = lwt, y = bwt) ) + 
  ggplot2::geom_point() + 
  ggplot2::facet_grid(smoke~.)

```
:::

::::


```{r facet-axes3}

birthwt |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = lwt, y = bwt) ) + 
  geom_point() +

```

```{r facet-axes4}
#| code-line-numbers: "4"
```

## Position adjustments {.smaller}

Useful for bar plots and histograms:

- `stack`: stack overlapping bars on top of each other (default).
- `identity`:  does nothing to overlapping bars but requires alpha.
  - Helpful for histograms but not bar plots.
- `fill`: stack overlapping bars and scale so the top is always at 1.
  - Helpful for bar plots but not histograms.
- `dodge`: place overlapping bars side-by-side.

. . .

Version for scatterplots when many points overlap:

- `position_nudge()`: move points by a fixed offset.
- `position_jitter()`: add a little random noise to every position.
- `position_jitterdodge()`: dodge points within groups, then add a little random noise.

## Position adjustments: Bar charts {.smaller}

```{r position-bar1}
#| code-line-numbers: "4"
#| output-location: "column"
#| fig-height: 1.7
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-align: center

birthwt |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = smoke, 
                      fill = race) ) + 
  ggplot2::geom_bar() # default = stack

```

. . .

```{r position-bar2}
#| code-line-numbers: "4"
#| output-location: "column"
#| fig-height: 1.7
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-align: center

birthwt |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = smoke, 
                      fill = race) ) + 
  ggplot2::geom_bar(position = "fill")

```

. . .

```{r position-bar3}
#| code-line-numbers: "4"
#| output-location: "column"

#| fig-width: 5

birthwt |>

                      fill = race) ) +

```

## Position adjustments: Histograms {.smaller}

```{r position-hist1}
#| code-line-numbers: "4-5"
#| output-location: "column"
#| fig-height: 1.7
#| fig-width: 5
```

## Scales {.smaller}
- Scales control how the aesthetic mappings of variables manifest visually in plots.
  - How a variable is translated into `color`, `size`, `shape`, etc.
- Every aesthetic has a default scale.

. . .

```{r scales-default}
#| code-line-numbers: "8-11"
#| output-location: "column"
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center

birthwt |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(
    aes(x = lwt, y = bwt)
    ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    aes(color = smoke)
    ) +
  # ggplot adds by default:
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous() + # x-axis
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous() + # y-axis
  ggplot2::scale_color_discrete() # color

```

## Overriding default scales {.smaller}
- `ggplot2` has syntax to override default scales.
- General naming scheme: `scales_['aesthetic']{style="color:red;"}_['scale']{style="color:red;"}.
  - `breaks` and `labels` are the main arguments used.

```{r scales1}
#| code-line-numbers: "4-12"
#| output-location: "column"
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-align: center

birthwt |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = lwt, y = bwt) ) +
  geom_point(aes(color = smoke) ) + 
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(50, 250, by = 25) 
    ) + 
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(500, 5500, by = 500) 
    ) + 
  scale_color_discrete(
    labels = c("Smoker" = "Current smoker", 
               "Nonsmoker" = "Current nonsmoker"))

```

## Color scales: ColorBrewer {.smaller}
- Discrete color scale with colors picked from [ColorBrewer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ColorBrewer).
  - Some colorblind friendly palettes (e.g., `Dark2`).

::::{.columns}

:::{.column .fragment .fade-in width="50%"}
```{r scales-brewer1}
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center

birthwt |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = lwt, y = bwt) ) +
  geom_point(aes(color = smoke) ) + 
  ggplot2::scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2")
```
:::

:::{.column .fragment .fade-in width="50%"}
```{r scale-brewer2}
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center

birthwt |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = lwt, y = bwt) ) +
  geom_point(aes(color = smoke) ) + 
  ggplot2::scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1")

```

## Color scales: Manual {.smaller}
- It is also possible to supply your own color palette.
  - `ggplot2` quick color [reference](https://sape.inf.usi.ch/quick-reference/ggplot2/colour).
- Or use a palette from a package: [wesanderson](https://github.com/karthik/wesanderson), [waRhol](https://github.com/alexskeels/waRhol), [ggsci](https://nanx.me/ggsci/), and more.
  - Check the [paletteer](https://github.com/EmilHvitfeldt/paletteer) package for a large, searchable collection.

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r scales-manual1}
#| code-line-numbers: "4-7"
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-align: center

birthwt |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = lwt, y = bwt) ) +
  geom_point(aes(color = race) ) +

    values = c("orangered1", 
               "mediumpurple2",

```
:::


## Themes
- [Themes](https://ggplot2-book.org/themes.html) allow you to customize non-data elements of your plot.
- `ggplot2` comes with [eight](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/communication.html#sec-themes) prespecified themes: `theme_*()`.
  - Change multiple aspects of the plot simultaneously.
- `theme()` lets you to change specific elements of the plot to your specification.
  - Text size, color, legend position, etc.

## `theme_*()` {.smaller}

```{r theme1}
#| code-line-numbers: "4"
#| output-location: "column"
#| fig-height: 2.1
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center

birthwt |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = lwt, y = bwt) ) +
  geom_point() + 
  ggplot2::theme_bw()

```

. . .

```{r theme2}
#| code-line-numbers: "4"
#| output-location: "column"
#| fig-height: 2.1
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center

birthwt |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = lwt, y = bwt) ) +
  geom_point() + 
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()

```

. . .

```{r theme3}
#| code-line-numbers: "4"
#| output-location: "column"
#| fig-height: 2.1
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center

birthwt |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = lwt, y = bwt) ) +
  geom_point() + 
  ggplot2::theme_classic()

```

## `theme()` {.smaller}

```{r theme4}
#| code-line-numbers: "4-10"
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center

birthwt |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = lwt, y = bwt) ) +
  geom_point(aes(color = smoke) ) + 
  ggplot2::theme_bw() + 
  ggplot2::theme(
    legend.position = "top", 
    legend.title = element_blank(), 
    legend.box.background = element_rect(color = "black"), 
    text = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10, color = "red", angle = 90, face = "bold")
  )

```

## Patchwork: Combining plots {.smaller}
- We often have many related plots that we want to combine into one figure.
- `+` combines plots, automatically choosing the number of rows/columns.
- `/` stacks plots vertically; `|` places plots side by side (and does not autowrap).

```{r patchwork1}
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Three plots of birth weight -- a histogram, a density plot, and a violin plot by race -- arranged by patchwork in a single row."

# need to load patchwork package for "+", "/", and "|" notation to work
histPlot.bwt + densityPlot.bwt + violinPlot.bwt.race

```

## Patchwork: Combining plots {.smaller}
- Add titles, captions, and control relative panel sizes with `plot_annotation()` and `plot_layout()`.

```{r patchwork2}
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Birth weight histogram and density plot placed side by side on top, with the violin plot by race spanning the bottom at twice the height of the row above, with an overall title and source caption."

(histPlot.bwt | densityPlot.bwt) / violinPlot.bwt.race + 
  patchwork::plot_annotation(
    title = "Birth weight: histogram, density, and violin plot by race",
    caption = "Source: MASS::birthwt"
    ) + 
  patchwork::plot_layout(
    heights = c(1, 2) # ratio of heights
    )

```

## Saving plots {.smaller}
- Once you've made a plot, you may want to save it to share with others or to include in a paper or presentation.

```{r saving-plots, eval = F}

ggplot2::ggsave(filename = here::here("output/YYYYMMDD_module03-birthwt-violinPlot.pdf"), 
                plot = violinPlot.bwt.race, 
                height = 6, 
                width = 12)

```

- File name conventions should be used (informative and dated).
- If `plot` is not specified, the most recent plot displayed is saved.
- If `height` and `width` aren't specified, the dimensions of the current plot are used.
  - Aspect ratios (width:height) of 2:1 or 4:3 are preferred.
- Saving to .pdf gives the highest resolution.
  - Although other file types are support (.png, .jpeg).

# Appendix {visibility="uncounted"}

## Why visualize? {visibility="uncounted"}
- Summarizing data is fundamental to statistics.
- Numeric summaries (mean, variance, correlation, etc.) are common and informative.
- Pairing numeric summaries with data visualizations provides deeper insights, some that may be missed by numerical analysis alone.

## Why visualize: 13 data sets {.smaller visibility="uncounted"}
::: notes
- 13 data sets, each with x, y coordinate pairs --> scatter plot each
- Same summary statistics
:::

```{r datasaurus-head}

head(datasauRus::datasaurus_dozen, n = 3)

```

. . .

```{r datasaurus-12plots-stats}

datasauRus::datasaurus_dozen |> 
  dplyr::summarise(.by = dataset, 
                   mean.x = mean(x), 
                   mean.y = mean(y), 
                   sd.x = sd(x), 
                   sd.y = sd(y), 
                   corr = round(cor(x,y), 2)
                   )

```

## Why visualize: 13 data sets {visibility="uncounted"}
::: notes
- Clearly very different scatter plots (viz) but the same summary statistics
:::

```{r datasaurus-12plots}
#| echo: FALSE
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Grid of 13 scatterplots from the Datasaurus Dozen dataset: a scattered cloud (away), concentric rings (bullseye), a ring (circle), a dinosaur outline (dino), grouped dot clusters (dots), horizontal bands (h_lines, high_lines), diagonal bands (slant_down, slant_up), a star outline (star), vertical bands (v_lines, wide_lines), and an X shape (x_shape)."

datasauRus::datasaurus_dozen |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, color = dataset)) +  
  ggplot2::geom_point() + 
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(.~dataset) + 
  ggplot2::theme_classic() + # change plot background
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "none") # remove legend

```

::: aside
From: [Same Stats, Different Graphs](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3025453.3025912)
:::

```{r datasaurus-bp1}
datasauRus::box_plots

datasauRus::box_plots_long |>

    .by = Plot,

                  probs = 0.25),

    )
```

```{r datasaurus-bp2}
#| echo: FALSE

datasauRus::box_plots_long |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(y = Values, x= Plot, color = Plot)) +
```

## Visualize in multiple ways {visibility="uncounted"}
::: notes
- Histogram shows differences in distributions
:::

```{r datasaurus-bp3}
#| echo: FALSE
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Grid comparing the same five groups (left, lines, normal, right, split): boxplots on top look nearly identical, but histograms below reveal very different shapes - from a smooth bell curve ('normal') to spiky, skewed, or multimodal patterns for the rest."

bpData.bp.datasaurus = datasauRus::box_plots_long |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(y = Values, color = Plot)) + 
  ggplot2::geom_boxplot() + 
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(.~Plot, nrow = 1) + 
  ggplot2::theme_classic() + 
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "none")

bpData.hist.datasaurus = datasauRus::box_plots_long |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = Values, fill = Plot)) + 
  ggplot2::geom_histogram() +  
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(.~Plot, nrow = 1) + 
  ggplot2::theme_classic() + 
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "none")

ggpubr::ggarrange(bpData.bp.datasaurus, bpData.hist.datasaurus, nrow = 2)


```

## Visualize with mappings {visibility="uncounted"}
::: notes
- Overall trend line is positive, but can see clusters that have negative trend lines (Simpson's Paradox)
- Color and shape show that there is a group variable explains these differences
:::


::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r simpson1}
#| echo: FALSE
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot with a fitted blue linear regression line, but the underlying data actually forms several distinct parallel diagonal stripes rather than one linear trend. The regression line passes through the overall cloud."

# centers for k-means clustering
ctrs = matrix(
  c(
    25,15,
    38,29,
    48,58,
    60,75,
    75,83
  ),
  byrow=TRUE,
  ncol=2
)

# filter data
simpsons = datasauRus::simpsons_paradox |> 
  dplyr::filter(dataset == "simpson_2", 30 < x, x < 75) |> 
  dplyr::select(-dataset)

simpsons |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point() + 
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = F) + 
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "none")

```
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment .fade-in}
```{r simpson2}
#| echo: FALSE
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot with data split into 5 groups by color/shape, each with its own fitted regression line. Once separated, each group shows a clear negative (downward) trend, revealing that the overall positive trend seen when all points were combined was an illusion caused by mixing distinct groups."

simpsons |> 
  dplyr::mutate(group = kmeans(simpsons, ctrs)$cluster |> as.character()) |> 
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, colour = group, shape = group)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point() + 
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = F) + 
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "top")

```
:::
:::

::::

:::{.fragment .fade-in}
- The overall trend line is positive, but when a third variable is added to the plot via `aes()` it is clear that within each group the trend line is negative.
:::
